content_list.content_text: Flashback to 1956. A series of short, low-budget British documentaries reaches London screens. As one London newspaper put it, "all the bearded boys in duffel coats and the girls in jeans with cropped hair in the city seem to converge" on the South Bank to watch "Free Cinema" films.

information.contentText:
After becoming one of the leading names of the Free Cinema movement in the 1950s, with documentaries such as Every Day Except Xmas, Lindsay Anderson shot This Sporting Life, his first feature film and one of the major achievements of the so-called British New Wave, a movement related to the Angry Young Men and, stylistically and thematically, a sibling of the French New Wave.

Set in the industrial north of England, the film was released at the height of the critical popularity of working-class dramas and turned Anderson into a top-tier director in Britain. This Sporting Life remains one of the few films to depict the dark side of athletes' lives, in this case rugby players.

content_list.content_text: The documentaries frankly tackled subjects such as amusement parks, dance halls, and youth clubs. In the context of British cinema at the time, they were pioneering works. For director and critic Lindsay Anderson (1923-1994), the 1950s were, for British cinema, a period of complacency and "lukewarm humanism". It was the era of John Mills war films and stoic dramas in which "chaps" like Jack Hawkins appeared smoking pipes.

quote.quote: I've taken a tip from the fish: biting the bait is never a good idea. I'm not getting married till I'm good and ready.
quote.author: Arthur Seaton (Albert Finney) in Saturday Night and Sunday Morning

content_list.content_text: The British New Wave was driven by a group of critics turned filmmakers who, in the late 1940s, were closely linked to the film magazine Sequence, at the University of Oxford, and later went on to write for Sight and Sound. Its leading figures were Lindsay Anderson, Karel Reisz (1926-2002), Tony Richardson (1928-1991), and Gavin Lambert (1924-2005). In their first feature films, the group resolutely turned its focus to the industrial north of Britain.

But the film most widely accepted as the starting point of the British New Wave was made by Jack Clayton (1921-1995), a director not linked to the Sequence group. The subversive northern working-class hero and the unprecedentedly direct treatment of sex and social class in Room at the Top (1958) set the template followed by Reisz in Saturday Night and Sunday Morning (1960), Richardson in The Loneliness of the Long Distance Runner (1962), and Anderson in This Sporting Life (1963).

information.contentTitle: Scenes from The Loneliness of the Long Distance Runner
information.contentText: The Loneliness of the Long Distance Runner portrays Britain in the late 1950s and early 1960s as an elitist place, where the upper classes enjoy many privileges while the lower classes endure bleak lives, and its Borstal system of detention centers for young offenders as a way of keeping workers in their place.

content_list.content_text: Like Clayton, John Schlesinger (1926-2003) also kept his distance from the core group, but his A Kind of Loving (1962), starring Alan Bates (1934-2003), follows the same pattern. All these films were made, as Richardson later wrote, with "a minimum of equipment, real locations, and a naturally unkempt look".

Most British New Wave films are adaptations of novels and plays, as is the case with Look Back in Anger (1959) and A Taste of Honey (1961) - both by Tony Richardson (1928-1991) - based respectively on Look Back in Anger, by John Osborne, and A Taste of Honey, by Shelagh Delaney.

information.contentTitle: Scenes from Saturday Night and Sunday Morning
information.contentText: Saturday Night and Sunday Morning (1960) was at the forefront of the British New Wave, portraying British working-class life seriously for the first time and dealing realistically with sex and abortion. It was one of the first "kitchen sink dramas" (dramas of the kitchen sink), which followed the success of the play Look Back in Anger.

content_list.content_text: The second is unusual for having a woman as its protagonist, played by newcomer Rita Tushingham (b. 1942). Its directors' Oxford education explains some critics' skepticism about the authenticity of British New Wave films. An article in The Guardian mocked the way these middle-class southern directors looked to the North in search of "the hard lives and thick accents that best suit their ideological leanings".

As expected, the energy of the British New Wave soon dissipated. Before leaving for Hollywood, Tony Richardson made the period extravaganza Tom Jones (1963). After Billy Liar (1963), Schlesinger turned his attention south with Darling (1965). The far-from-prolific Anderson made no other film until if.... (1968). But the spirit of the New Wave transformed British cinema forever. Its influence can be seen in the films of Ken Loach (b. 1936), Mike Leigh (b. 1943), and Terence Davies (b. 1945) and, more recently, in the work of Andrea Arnold (b. 1961), Lynne Ramsay (b. 1969), and Pawel Pawlikowski (b. 1957).
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Geoffrey Macnab, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp.

movies.title: Saturday Night and Sunday Morning
movies.overview: A 22-year-old factory worker lets loose on the weekends: drinking, brawling, and dating two women, one of whom is older and married.

movies.title: This Sporting Life
movies.overview: In Northern England in the early 1960s, Frank Machin is mean, tough and ambitious enough to become an immediate star in the rugby league team run by local employer Weaver.

movies.original_title: The Loneliness of the Long Distance Runner
movies.title: The Loneliness of the Long Distance Runner
movies.overview: A rebellious youth, sentenced to a boy's reformatory for robbing a bakery, rises through the ranks of the institution through his prowess as a long distance runner. During his solitary runs, reveries of his life and times before his incarceration lead him to re-evaluate his privileged status as the Governor's prize runner.

movies.title: A Kind of Loving
movies.overview: As Vic Brown vacillates between infatuation and disinterest for his co-worker Ingrid Rothwell, she  finds out that she is pregnant and Vic has to reconcile how he thought his life would go with what life actually has in store for him.

movies.title: Darling
movies.overview: The swinging London, early sixties. Beautiful but shallow, Diana Scott is a professional advertising model, a failed actress, a vocationally bored woman, who toys with the affections of several men while gaining fame and fortune.

movies.title: Terminus
movies.overview: This fly on the wall-style documentary from 1961 won an Oscar for best documentary, and shows the changing patterns of human emotions during 24 hours in the life of Waterloo Station.

content_list.title: Timeline of Events from 1960 to 1969
content_list.description: Brazil catches the world's attention with its Cinema Novo, the sexual revolution of the '60s is reflected in film, psychological horror gains ground, and science fiction, with 2001: A Space Odyssey, wins over audiences and critics.
